title: Ebola Outbreak Reaches Nigeria, a Fourth Country, in the Fastest-Spreading Outbreak on Record
excerpt: Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in over a decade as the Bundibugyo-strain outbreak sweeping Congo becomes the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded.
content:
Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday, October 20, becoming the fourth African country reached by an outbreak that health officials describe as the most geographically extensive and the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record.

The patient is a woman in Abuja, the capital, who had traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo and transited through Uganda, according to Reuters. She arrived back in Nigeria on October 5, developed symptoms on October 7, and was hospitalized on October 11. She tested positive on October 19 and is being treated in isolation. Health officials have identified 44 contacts — most of them healthcare workers — who are being monitored.

An outbreak now in its sixth month

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus and began in Congo in mid-May 2026. Congolese authorities have recorded more than 9,500 cases across eight provinces, with 4,646 deaths — a fatality rate of roughly 50 percent. Kenya reported nine cases this month. Officials describe the outbreak as the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, behind only the 2014–2016 West African epidemic.

Africa CDC Director General Jean Kaseya called the outbreak “an extremely serious threat,” Reuters reported.

No approved vaccine or treatment for this strain

Unlike the Zaire strain of Ebola, the Bundibugyo species has no approved treatment and no approved vaccine. That leaves rapid case detection, isolation, and contact tracing as the main tools health authorities have to contain it — which is why officials moved quickly to identify and monitor the Abuja patient's 44 contacts.

What it means for readers here

No cases connected to this outbreak have been reported in the United States, according to the Reuters and Associated Press reports. Webb Watch 956 is following the outbreak because of its scale: a fast-moving, multi-country epidemic is the kind of development that can change quickly, and we will update this story as new information is confirmed.

Update — October 21, 2026

The World Health Organization formally confirmed Nigeria's case in a statement released October 20, calling Nigeria the fifth country to detect the Bundibugyo strain since the outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May 2026 — counting the DRC, Uganda, Kenya, the Netherlands, and Nigeria. That count adds one country to the four African nations in this story's headline, with a case detected in the Netherlands linked to the DRC outbreak.

WHO also released updated regional figures: Congolese health authorities had recorded more than 9,500 cases and more than 4,200 deaths as of October 18. Kenya has reported nine confirmed cases linked to an imported infection, the organization said.

The UN health agency said it is assisting Nigeria's response through case investigations, contact tracing, and protective-equipment supplies, and it advised against imposing travel or trade restrictions on affected countries, saying risk assessments will continue to be reassessed.

Update — October 21, 2026 (evening)

Uganda's Health Ministry clarified Tuesday that the Abuja patient had traveled to the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo for business and only transited through Uganda without showing symptoms — and that Uganda currently has no active Ebola cases, according to El País and Reuters. Nigeria's health ministry said investigators are still reconstructing her full travel and exposure history. Separately, Africa CDC Director General Jean Kaseya said Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa, calling for "urgent action and political leadership at the highest level," Reuters reported.
